messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For as long as he could remember, Amir had prided himself on precision. At fifty-four, working as a software engineer in a downtown office tower, he spent his days refining algorithms, isolating variables, and eliminating bugs. He believed that if you understood the system well enough, you could control the outcome. That belief had been shattered one evening three years ago, when he had stayed late to finish a deployment. A colleague—a man Amir had trusted, someone who held a senior position in the company—had asked to speak with him privately in a storage room. Once the door clicked shut, the colleague pinned him against a metal shelf and assaulted him. Amir had frozen. He had not screamed. He had not fought back. And in the weeks that followed, that stillness became the detail he could not forgive himself for.

In the immediate aftermath, Amir told no one. He finished the deployment, drove home, and showered for forty minutes. He told himself it was a misunderstanding, that if he just kept working, the feeling would pass. But it did not pass. Within a month, he found himself unable to walk past the storage room on his floor. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, adding twelve minutes to his commute each morning, because the stairwell door was on the opposite side of the building. He began avoiding the company cafeteria when he saw anyone in a suit—anyone who looked like an authority figure, anyone who might have the power to trap him in a room again. The colleague had worn a dark blazer that night, and now Amir found himself tensing at the sight of any uniform: police officers on the street, security guards in the lobby, even the maintenance staff in their branded polo shirts. He knew it made no sense. He knew a janitor was not a threat. But his body did not care.

The sirens started to matter about six weeks afterward. An ambulance passed his apartment window one Saturday morning, and Amir found himself on the floor, heart pounding, certain that something terrible was happening again. He began checking the street before leaving his building. He started mapping routes in his head that avoided hospitals, fire stations, any place emergency vehicles might congregate. His world began to shrink. He stopped going to the grocery store after dark, because that was when the sirens seemed loudest. He stopped accepting invitations to dinner with male friends, because being alone with a man—any man, even one he had known for twenty years—made his throat close up. He told himself it was temporary. He told himself he was being careful.

But careful became a cage. Amir came to believe that he was never truly safe unless he was in his apartment, with the door locked and the blinds drawn. He developed a habit of scanning every room he entered: checking the exits, noting the positions of other people, cataloging potential weapons or obstacles. He did it automatically now, even in his own office, even when he was alone. He had become certain that danger was always lurking, that the next attack could come from anywhere, and that if he let his guard down for a single second, he would be caught again. The worst part was that he knew it was irrational. He could feel the mismatch—the empty hallway, the quiet coffee shop, the harmless colleague—and still his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and he would have to leave.

The injustice of it gnawed at him constantly. He had reported nothing. The colleague still worked on the same floor. Amir had to coordinate code reviews with him, attend meetings with him, pretend nothing had happened. He had come to believe that the system had failed before he even tried it—that no one would believe a fifty-four-year-old man who had not fought back. And so the unfairness sat inside him like a stone, growing heavier each time he had to shake the man’s hand at a stand-up. He blamed himself, too. He replayed the moment again and again: the way he had stood there, the way he had said nothing, the way he had walked out afterward and acted as if everything was fine. He was certain that the assault had happened because of the way he had acted—or failed to act. He had lost faith in his own judgment, and worse, he had lost the ability to feel anything normal. Joy felt foreign. Grief felt like a locked room. He told his therapist in the first session that he could not remember the last time he had laughed without checking over his shoulder first.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a performance review. His manager had noticed his declining productivity, his avoidance of collaborative work, his refusal to attend team-building events. Amir was told that if things did not improve, his position might be at risk. That threat—losing the one structure that still anchored his days—frightened him more than the memories. He came to therapy wanting to find a way to function again. But underneath that, what he really wanted was to stop living in a world where every siren meant danger, where every closed door meant a trap, and where the man who hurt him still walked the same hallways while Amir stayed frozen in place.
